Use case: scientific-educational. Create a high resolution landscape raster study infographic, approximately 3:2 aspect ratio. All content in English. Match the supplied existing T2.1 repository images as STYLE REFERENCES, not edit targets: same white pale-blue graph-paper background, wide rounded dark navy header with bold white humanist sans-serif type and teal InterSystems IRIS ObjectScript badge, thin navy/cyan rounded panel outlines, blue gradient numbered section tabs, purple/lavender concept cards, pale cyan table cells, teal arrows, green success ticks, amber warning cards, navy-outlined yellow padlocks, database cylinders, document/list icons and small flat illustrated laptop users. Dense but highly legible like the references: three horizontal information-rich bands, large hierarchy, compact explanatory sentences, clear margins. No photorealism, no decorative filler, no watermark. Render exact technical text and punctuation carefully. Keep this a companion sheet to the references, not a reproduction of their text.
Title: "T2.1: Ensures Data Integrity | Lock modes & lifetime"
Band 1 title: "1. Shared vs. exclusive: who can acquire a lock?"
Draw two laptop users sharing teal S padlocks and an exclusive purple lock waiting. Include compatibility matrix for DIFFERENT processes on SAME resource:
Held / Request shared / Request exclusive
Shared / Allowed / Wait
Exclusive / Wait / Wait
Code labels: 'LOCK +^Demo(1)#"S":5' and 'LOCK +^Demo(1):5'.
Caption: "S controls compatibility. Without S, the lock is exclusive."
Warning: "Cooperating code must request the same lock. Direct SET/KILL does not automatically obey an application lock."
Band 2 title: "2. Unlock timing inside a transaction"
Three parallel mini timelines all start TSTART -> LOCK +^Demo(1).
A: 'LOCK -^Demo(1)' -> amber "Delock: release pending" -> TCOMMIT -> open padlock.
B: 'LOCK -^Demo(1)#"I"' -> open padlock "Release now" -> TCOMMIT.
C: 'LOCK -^Demo(1)#"D"' -> note "Restore previous unlock state; first use can release immediately."
Small amber note: "I and D are unlock modifiers, not shared/exclusive modes. D is not a synonym for the default unlock."
Footer within band: "Examples assume lock count 1. A held application lock still needs matching unlocks."
Band 3 title: "3. E means eligible to escalate"
Draw sibling lock nodes ^Batch(1,1), ^Batch(1,2), ... -> large parent lock ^Batch(1).
Code: 'LOCK +^Batch(1,i)#"E":5'
Caption: "Default threshold 1000: request 1001 attempts the parent lock. If successful, child entries merge into a counted parent lock."
Warning: "Ordinary LOCK does not escalate. Match E on unlock: LOCK -^Batch(1,i)#\"E\". Shared and escalating can combine as SE."
Bottom takeaway green strip: "Compatibility (S), release timing (I/D), and escalation (E) answer different questions."
Do not add any other technical assertions.

Title: "T2.1: Ensures Data Integrity | SQL locks & the lock table"
Band 1 title: "1. Lock table is a registry; table lock is a scope"
Left illustrated list icon: "Lock table (memory)" with columns Resource / Owner / Mode, sample schematic entries "Orders row 7 / A / Exclusive" and "Orders row 9 / B / Exclusive". Caption "Tracks locks, owners, counts and waiting. Inspect it in Management Portal."
Right two SQL Orders tables: row 7 alone padlocked vs entire table covered by padlock. Labels "Row lock: narrow protection, more concurrency" and "Table lock: broad protection, fewer entries". Caption "Both are recorded in the lock table."
Band 2 title: "2. SQL vs. explicit ObjectScript locking"
Compact comparison: "SQL INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE: automatic row protection unless %NOLOCK; transaction locks last to transaction end." / "ObjectScript LOCK: application chooses the resource name; matching lock/unlock and timeout handling are explicit." Small caption "They use IRIS locking; an arbitrary application lock name need not match SQL's generated lock name."
Visual worked example headed "Escalation example: Orders, threshold 1000"
A locks rows 1...1000 -> A requests row 1001 -> if compatible, broad Orders table lock.
B requests an exclusive lock on row 1500: "Before: can succeed" / "After: waits or times out".
Amber note: "Escalation can conflict or deadlock. A broad lock does not block every kind of read: isolation and compatibility matter."
Band 3 title: "3. %NOLOCK: suppress automatic DML row locks"
Purple code card exactly:
"UPDATE %NOLOCK Demo.Account"
"SET Balance = Balance + 10"
"WHERE ID = 7;"
Adjacent bullets:
"Also available for INSERT and DELETE."
"Requires the namespace %NOLOCK administrative privilege."
"Use only with exclusive access secured, e.g. a controlled single-writer load or a deliberately held table lock."
Amber caution: "Without another protection strategy, concurrent writes can race. %NOLOCK does not disable journaling or transactions."
Small note: "For SELECT, learn IRIS isolation levels and %NOLOCK is not a SQL Server-style FROM-table hint."
Bottom green takeaway: "Row/table = granularity. Lock table = registry. %NOLOCK = responsibility for protection."
Do not add additional technical assertions.
